subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Write the reaction showing α-halogenation of carboxylic acid and give its name.

mark_split.label: The name and the α-hydrogen condition

verification.note: Unit 17 (Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.112-115, from the shaded sub-box "ALDEHYDES, KETONES, AND CARBOXYLIC ACIDS" of printed chapter 12 ("12. ORGANIC CHEMISTRY"), which prints this question on book p.112 as VSAQ 1. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK WORDING: the printed answer reads "Carboxylic acids having an α-hydrogen position on treatment with chlorine (or) bromine ... to give α-halo carboxylic acids" — a sentence with a word missing after "α-hydrogen"; it is rewritten here as "a carboxylic acid with an α-hydrogen is halogenated at the α-carbon". BOOK SPELLING: the printed name is "Hell-volhard zelinsky"; the three chemists are Hell, Volhard and Zelinsky, so the name is written here as Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky. BOOK GAP: the printed equation shows only the halogen and red phosphorus and stops there. The reaction actually goes through an acyl halide, and the α-halo ACID is obtained only after a water work-up, so step (ii) H₂O is added from NCERT. BOOK GAP: the printed answer never states the exception — an acid with no α-hydrogen (benzoic acid, formic acid) does not undergo the reaction at all — so that is added. CROSS-UNIT NEIGHBOUR: unit 7 card ts_ipe_c2_va_pcl5_reactions covers CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl; that is a different reaction (the –OH is replaced) and does not overlap this one (an α-hydrogen is replaced).

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question
Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids — 2 marks

steps.label: The reaction with its conditions
lines: A carboxylic acid with an α-hydrogen is
halogenated at the α-carbon by chlorine or
bromine, with a small amount of red
phosphorus, and is then treated with water.
steps.why: Red phosphorus and the halogen first make a small amount of PCl₃ or PBr₃, which turns the acid into its acyl halide. Only the acyl halide has an α-hydrogen acidic enough to be replaced, so the halogen goes to the α-carbon and not to the –OH group. The water at the end turns the α-halo acyl halide back into the α-halo acid.
common_mistakes: Putting the halogen on the –OH group. That gives an acyl halide; here the halogen replaces an α-hydrogen.
Leaving out red phosphorus. Without it the acid is not halogenated at the α-carbon at all.
Forgetting the HCl or HBr on the product side. One hydrogen leaves for every halogen that enters.
steps.memory_tip: Halogen plus red phosphorus, then water. The halogen bonds to the carbon next to –COOH.
steps.margin_note: Write the reagents red P and H₂O ABOVE the arrow on your answer sheet; they are printed in brackets here only because a plain line cannot carry text over an arrow. Both conditions are needed for this mark.

steps.label: The name and the α-hydrogen condition
lines: The product is an α-halo carboxylic acid.
It is used to make α-amino acids and
Condition: the acid must have an α-hydrogen.
Benzoic acid C₆H₅COOH and formic acid HCOOH
have no α-hydrogen, so they do not react.
steps.why: The α-hydrogen is the whole condition of the reaction, so naming it is what turns a remembered name into a usable rule. Benzoic acid has a benzene ring on the carbonyl carbon and formic acid has only a hydrogen there, so neither has a carbon next to –COOH carrying a hydrogen, and neither gives the reaction.
common_mistakes: Spelling the name as one person. It is three: Hell, Volhard and Zelinsky.
Writing that any carboxylic acid gives the reaction. An acid with no α-hydrogen, such as benzoic acid, does not.
steps.memory_tip: HVZ = Hell, Volhard, Zelinsky, and the H at the front is a reminder that an α-hydrogen is required.
steps.margin_note: The name alone is worth this mark, but add the one-line α-hydrogen condition; it costs one line and it is what the examiner reads for understanding.

insider_note: The name Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky is half the marks on this two-mark question, so write it even if you are unsure of the equation. The most common loss is putting the halogen on the –OH group instead of on the α-carbon.
